questions.question: What basic components make up a pinhole camera?
options: A lens at the front, a mirror at the back, and a closed box
An empty, closed box with a tiny hole on the front face and a screen on the back face
Two parallel glass plates inside a hollow tube with an eyepiece
A transparent triangular prism inside a dark cylinder

questions.question: What are the characteristics of the image produced by a standard pinhole camera, and what happens if you add more holes?
options: The image is bright and upright; adding more holes makes it larger.
The image is dim and inverted; adding more holes produces multiple images.
The image is bright and inverted; adding more holes makes it sharper.
The image is dim and upright; adding more holes makes it disappear.

questions.question: What is the effect of making the hole in a pinhole camera larger?
options: The image becomes brighter but blurred because more light passes through in more directions.
The image becomes dimmer but sharper because fewer light rays overlap.
The image becomes smaller and inverted because of increased diffraction.
The image disappears completely because the light rays cancel each other out.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true about how light from an object passes through a lens?
options: Light only passes through the very centre of a lens to form an image.
Some light from every point on an object passes through every part of a lens.
Only light from the top of an object passes through the upper half of a lens.
Light must pass through both the front and back surfaces at the exact same spot to be focused.

questions.question: How does a convex lens affect light rays, and what is the meeting point of these rays called?
options: It refracts light rays so they travel away from each other; the point they diverge from is called the normal.
It reflects light rays back to the source; the point they return to is called the origin.
It refracts light rays so they travel more towards each other; the point where they meet is called a focus.
It absorbs light rays to prevent scattering; the point of maximum absorption is called the shadow.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the size, orientation, and position of a reflection in a plane mirror compared to the object?
options: It is smaller, inverted, and closer to the mirror than the object.
It is larger, upright, and twice as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
It is the same size, upright, and the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front.
It is the same size, inverted, and located directly on the surface of the mirror.

questions.question: When an object is facing us, how does its reflection in a plane mirror appear?
options: It appears vertically upside down.
It appears laterally inverted (left and right are swapped).
It appears completely unchanged in orientation.
It appears magnified and rotated by 90 degrees.

questions.question: Why are mirror reflections classified as virtual images?
options: They can be projected onto a screen placed behind the mirror.
They appear where light rays actually cross and meet in physical space.
They are produced by light rays that only travel in straight lines after reflecting.
They appear where light rays seem to have come from, not where they actually come from.

questions.question: What determines the colour an object appears to be when viewed in white or coloured light?
options: The chemical temperature of the light source hitting its surface.
The speed at which light reflects off the object's surface.
The amounts of red, green, and blue light it is reflecting.
The total amount of light that passes directly through the object.

questions.question: Why does a white object look red when red light is shone on it?
options: It absorbs all red light and reflects other colours.
It reflects all colours of light, so it looks the same colour as the incident light.
It converts the incident red light into white light.
White objects can only reflect light when the room is completely dark.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes what happens to light that is not reflected by an object, and how black objects behave?
options: Unreflected light is scattered; black objects scatter all colours of light.
Unreflected light is refracted; black objects refract all colours of light.
Unreflected light is absorbed; black objects absorb all colours of light.
Unreflected light is transmitted; black objects transmit all colours of light.

questions.question: What happens to a ray of light when it enters a transparent material (like glass) from air at an angle to the normal?
options: It turns towards the normal.
It turns away from the normal.
It continues in a straight line without changing direction.
It is completely reflected back into the air.

questions.question: When light leaves a transparent material and re-enters the air at an angle, how does its path change?
options: It bends directly along the normal line.
It turns towards the normal.
It turns away from the normal.
It stops refracting and travels in a circle.

questions.question: What is the path of a light ray that enters and leaves a block of glass with parallel sides?
options: It is bent at a right angle and leaves perpendicular to its original path.
It ends up in its original direction, but is displaced to the side.
It is completely absorbed inside the glass and does not exit.
It exits in a random direction depending on the thickness of the glass.

questions.question: How can you create a secondary colour of light, and what happens when all three primary colours of light are mixed in equal amounts?
options: Mix unequal amounts of three primary colours; they make black.
Mix equal amounts of two primary colours; all three mixed in equal amounts makes white.
Mix a primary colour with black; all three mixed in equal amounts makes yellow.
Mix any colour with white light; all three mixed in equal amounts makes a shadow.

questions.question: How do display screens produce a wide range of different colours?
options: They contain tiny liquid prisms that rotate to filter white light.
They use tiny red, green, and blue lights (pixels) that vary in brightness.
They reflect ambient light using miniature mirrors of different shapes.
They dynamically paint chemical dyes onto the glass surface.
